chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Safwan ibn Yahya from Abu Jarir, Zakariyya ibn Idris al-Qummi, who said:
I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who leads a group in prayer who dislike that he should recite 'Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim' aloud, so he said: 'He should not recite it aloud.'

And as for what Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Ali al-Halabi and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man and Muhammad ibn Sinan and 'Abd Allah ibn Muskhan from Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Halabi from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him):
They asked him about one who recites 'Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim' when he intends to recite the Opening of the Book. He said: 'Yes, if he wishes, secretly; and if he wishes, aloud.'
They said: 'Does he recite it together with the other Surah?' He said: 'No.'

This is applicable to one who is in a voluntary prayer and has already recited part of the other Surah and intends to recite the remainder; at that time, he does not recite 'Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim'.
And that which clarifies this is what has been narrated:

key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

ai.seo_question: Should an Imam recite Bismillah aloud in prayer if the congregation dislikes it?
ai.summary: This passage from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the juristic debate regarding the audibility of reciting *Bismillah* at the start of Surah Al-Fatiha, highlighting the principle of *ikhtiyar* (choice) between silent and audible recitation. The text resolves apparent contradictions by contextualizing the prohibition of repeating *Bismillah* within a continuous Surah reading, a nuance critical to Shia fiqh regarding *qira'at* in both obligatory and voluntary prayers. It underscores the flexibility granted to the worshipper while maintaining structural integrity in Quranic recitation.
